item.title: China's search for U.S. airmen lost along Hump Route keeps WWII bonds alive
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
China's search for U.S. airmen lost along Hump Route keeps WWII bonds alive A document confirming the transfer of the U.S. airmen remains found along Hump Route is signed, witnessed by Chinese and American representatives, during a handover ceremony in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Nov. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Xu Bingjie) CHENGDU, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- Two Chinese honor guards carried a box containing human remains to a table and carefully set it down. U.S. Chief Warrant Officer Christine Bilas then gently placed a folded American national flag on top of this box. "Bring them home," said U.S. Navy Captain Colin Alexander Eliot, a forensic expert with the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA), as he watched the transfer ceremony at Jianchuan Museum in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, on Tuesday. U.S. Navy Commander Gregory Pavone then lifted the box from the table. Inside the box were eight bone fragments recovered from a glacier more than 5,000 meters above sea level in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. Believed to be the remains of American airmen who went missing while helping China fight Japanese aggression during World War II (WWII), these bone fragments had lain in the mountains for more than 80 years. Their identities have yet to be confirmed. The handover followed three expeditions over more than two years by a Chinese civilian search team, part of a decades-long effort by China and the United States to account for missing American military personnel. THREE TRIPS TO THE GLACIER Cering Qoizha, deputy curator of Jianchuan Museum's branch in Chongqing, southwest China, set out in 2024 to search for wartime aircraft wreckage and human remains in the glaciers of Nyingchi, Xizang. A Tibetan from Sichuan's Garze Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, he enlisted his two elder brothers and several local guides for these expeditions. The first attempt was cut short by a damaged cable crossing over a river. After the crossing was rebuilt, the team returned and found aircraft wreckage. It was not until their third trip that they discovered the bone fragments. The journey took them through forests and swamps, across icy rivers and up steep cliffs, where bears, hidden crevasses and ice holes posed constant dangers. On the glacier, decades of freezing and thawing had left the remains trapped beneath rocks. "We could only lie on the ground and use our hands and branches to turn over the rocks and search carefully," Cering Qoizha recalled. The team eventually recovered eight fragments. He had led an earlier expedition that found American aircrew remains in Xizang in 2015. "The crews of the Hump Route gave their lives to support China's resistance against Japanese aggression and lay alone on the glaciers for decades," Cering Qoizha said. "They were heroes. Bringing them back from the glaciers is something I wanted to do, and something I should do." U.S. honor guards receive the box containing the U.S. airmen remains found along Hump Route during a handover ceremony in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Nov. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Xu Bingjie) HUMAN COST OF THE HUMP After Japanese forces occupied Myanmar in 1942 and cut off the Yunnan-Myanmar road, which was China's last major overland supply link to the outside world, China and the United States established air routes connecting the state of Assam in northeastern India with Kunming in southwest China. Known as the Hump Route, this air corridor across the Himalayas became a vital lifeline for Allied supplies supporting China's resistance against Japanese aggression from 1942 to 1945. The route featured snow-covered mountains, deep gorges, glaciers and tropical forests. Violent air currents, low air pressure, hail, freezing weather conditions and attacks by Japanese aircraft made the journey perilous. So many planes crashed along the route that crews came to call it the "Aluminum Trail." More than 1,000 Chinese and American aircrew lost their lives along the route. With the high mountains and glaciers making searches exceptionally difficult, many of their remains have never been recovered. "Every day felt like the last," Chinese pilot Zhou Bing, who flew more than 110 round trips along the route, once recalled. Friends who were together one day could be gone the next, he said. The airlift also depended on the labor and sacrifices of ordinary Chinese people. At Jianchuan Museum, enormous stone rollers weighing between eight and 15 tonnes recall the construction of wartime airfields in Sichuan and Yunnan, both in China's southwest. Without access to modern road rollers, dozens or even hundreds of workers had to pull these heavy stones to prepare runways. Some were injured or killed while working under harsh wartime conditions. Chinese military personnel and civilians also monitored Japanese aircraft movements, providing American forces with information on their numbers, types, altitudes and directions when ground radar coverage was limited. This photo taken on Nov. 9, 2026 shows tourists visiting the Hall of the Heroes of the Flying Tigers of the Jianchuan Museum in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province. (Xinhua/Xu Bingjie) KEEPING THE SEARCH ALIVE For Fan Jianchuan, curator of the privately run Jianchuan Museum, searching for the missing American airmen is a way of repaying a debt of gratitude. "When a country, or a person, faces the greatest danger and hardship, having friends come to help is very important," he said. The museum began searching for wartime aircraft wreckage in Sichuan more than 20 years ago, later extending its expeditions to the remote glaciers of Xizang. "The Hump Route crews deserve to be remembered and thanked forever," Fan said. "In practical terms, that means finding their remains in China and returning them to the American side." China and the United States have cooperated in searching for American military personnel missing during WWII since the 1970s. In 2008, China's Ministry of National Defense and the U.S. Department of Defense signed a memorandum of understanding in Shanghai, establishing a formal mechanism for this work. At Tuesday's ceremony, an official with the general office of the Central Military Commission (CMC) said the joint efforts to recover the remains of missing U.S. servicemen were a testament to the two countries' history of fighting side by side against Japanese fascism during WWII. China has long supported the search on humanitarian grounds and is willing to continue practical cooperation with the United States in this field, the official said, adding that such efforts could contribute positively to building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability. Another official with the Office for International Military Cooperation of the CMC said investigation and joint working teams had conducted surveys and excavations in more than 100 locations across China, drawing support from local governments and residents. As the wartime stories of the Flying Tigers and Hump Route became more widely known, growing numbers of Chinese civilians joined the searches, the official said, citing Jianchuan Museum as a notable example. The official said the expanding involvement of ordinary people echoed the two countries' wartime cooperation and showed that "the hope of China-U.S. relations lies in the people." Pavone also spoke of the longstanding cooperation. "These joint efforts have been going on for decades and are one of the most durable areas of cooperation between our two militaries," he said, thanking the museum, local authorities and Chinese military and diplomatic agencies for their contributions. The remains still await identification. After the remains reach the United States, the DPAA will conduct DNA testing, examine historical evidence, and compare military records. Families will be notified only after identification is confirmed. Following the ceremony, Chinese and U.S. representatives visited the Hall of the Heroes of the Flying Tigers, which commemorates the Flying Tigers and other American servicemen who assisted China during WWII. A wall there bears ceramic portraits of 248 American servicemen. Among the thousands of artifacts on display are personal belongings donated by veterans. One donor was Robert Gruber, an elderly American veteran who visited in 2005 while the exhibition was being prepared. When he learned that the exhibition would showcase items related to WWII American servicemen, he was moved to tears. Gruber died not long after returning to the United States, but his belongings remain on display. They include a portrait of him in his youth in military attire and a cherished photograph of his girlfriend, kept in a frame made from the wreckage of a Japanese aircraft. The exhibition has received more than 10 million visitors over two decades. Among the messages in its guestbooks is one from a Chinese visitor: "May the people of China and the United States remember history and cherish peace." Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. item.title: From Beijing to Shenzhen: China's push for a more connected, dynamic Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
From Beijing to Shenzhen: China's push for a more connected, dynamic Asia-Pacific BEIJING, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen, south China, from Nov. 18 to 19, marking the first time in 12 years that China is hosting the APEC meeting, following Beijing in 2014. The Beijing meeting endorsed a vision of an integrated, innovative, and interconnected Asia-Pacific, calling for closer links in infrastructure, trade, and people-to-people exchanges. Over the past 12 years, China has worked with other APEC economies to advance that vision, expanding cooperation from transport and trade facilitation to digital and green development. This year's gathering, to be held under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," will focus on three priority areas identified by China -- openness, innovation, and cooperation -- and is expected to help regional economies deepen economic ties and foster new drivers of growth. People walk past an APEC-themed installation at Gangxia North Metro Station in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Mao Siqian) ADVANCING CONNECTIVITY At Yantian Port in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, nearly 100 international shipping routes operate each week, 53 of them connecting the port with other APEC economies. The flow of goods through the port reflects the growing connectivity and deepening economic ties between China and the wider region. Connectivity was a priority of China's 2014 APEC host year. At the Beijing meeting, leaders and representatives endorsed China's proposal to establish the APEC Cooperation Network on Green Supply Chain and approved the establishment of its first pilot center in north China's Tianjin. The center officially opened in June 2015 to promote green procurement and supply-chain assessment. The Green Supply Chain Network has grown into a key platform for regional cooperation on green trade. Trade agreements have also translated integration into business opportunities. The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), which came into force in 2022, has provided a foundation for deeper cooperation toward prosperity, resilience, and sustainability. RCEP binds ASEAN's 10 members at that time with China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand into the largest free trade zone in the world by population and GDP share. By lowering tariffs and harmonizing trade rules, RCEP is estimated to further boost intra-regional trade significantly and strengthen integrated regional supply chains. Alongside RCEP, the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area (CAFTA) has been significantly upgraded under CAFTA 3.0, which was signed at the 28th ASEAN-China Summit in October 2025. The new version expands the traditional trade pact far beyond tariff reduction. With nine new areas covering the digital economy, green economy and supply chain connectivity, among others, CAFTA 3.0 marks a milestone in economic cooperation that strengthens collective resilience amid global uncertainty. An aerial drone photo taken on April 13, 2026 shows a train of the China-Laos Railway, departing from Kunming of southwest China's Yunnan Province, arriving in Vientiane, Laos. (Photo by Xia Ningqin/Xinhua) China has also actively promoted infrastructure in the region. Jointly built and operated by China and Laos, the China-Laos Railway links Kunming in southwest China's Yunnan Province with the Lao capital Vientiane, providing landlocked Laos with a rail link to China and access to wider regional markets. Since operation in December 2021, it has carried more than 20.77 million tonnes of import and export goods worth over 100.4 billion yuan (about 15 billion U.S. dollars). The flow goes both ways: durians, mangosteens and other tropical fruits travel north, while Chinese machinery and electronics move south, bringing producers and markets across the region closer together. FOSTERING NEW GROWTH As regional connections have expanded, cooperation has moved beyond trade to encompass technologies and industries that will help shape future growth. At the 2014 Beijing meeting, APEC leaders and representatives endorsed the Accord on Innovative Development, Economic Reform and Growth, highlighting innovation and economic reform as drivers of regional growth. Trade data point to the growing importance of technology in regional economic ties. In 2025, China's high-tech exports to other APEC economies rose 8.1 percent to 4.63 trillion yuan (about 694 billion dollars), according to the General Administration of Customs. Shenzhen's growing AI sector offers a glimpse of the technological capabilities China can bring to regional cooperation. By the end of 2025, the city had more than 2,600 AI enterprises above designated size, with core AI industry revenue of about 220 billion yuan (about 32.97 billion dollars). At APEC business and AI forums in June 2026, participants from 13 APEC economies discussed AI applications and cross-border cooperation, while institutions from China, South Korea, Indonesia and other economies signed agreements on technology commercialization and cross-border industrial parks. This photo taken on July 4, 2026 shows an embodied intelligence robot displayed at AIR Design House in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Liang Xu) Antonio Basilio, director of the APEC Business Advisory Council Secretariat, said China's experience demonstrated the importance of translating technological innovation into practical economic applications, particularly in manufacturing, logistics, agriculture and services. These technological advances are also reflected in Shenzhen's export mix. In 2025, electric vehicles, lithium-ion batteries, photovoltaic products, AI-powered products, and medical instruments and equipment together accounted for 25.6 percent of Shenzhen's exports to other APEC economies. Chinese technology and investment are contributing to industrial development across the region. In Malaysia, Chinese battery maker EVE Energy has brought the second phase of its lithium battery plant into operation, the Southeast Asian country's first such large-scale factory. Located in northwestern Malaysia, the facility has an annual production capacity of 680 million cylindrical battery cells. In Thailand, BYD's Rayong plant has an annual production capacity of 150,000 vehicles and employs more than 6,000 people, about 95 percent of them Thai nationals. Mackenzie Lang, CEO of the Australia-China Youth Group, described Shenzhen as "a city everybody across the world now associates with technological innovation and economic development." He expressed hope that this year's APEC meeting would foster stronger regional economic ties and investment. SHARING PROSPERITY China's expanding market offers companies from other APEC economies opportunities to reach Chinese consumers and build lasting partnerships, while providing regional partners with much-needed expertise and capital. Shenzhen's growing economic ties with the region are a snapshot of this broader cooperation. In the first half of 2026, the city's trade with other APEC economies reached 1.98 trillion yuan (about 296.8 billion dollars), up 33 percent year on year, while investment by local enterprises in other APEC members accounted for nearly 60 percent of Shenzhen's total outbound investment. Meanwhile, the China International Import Expo (CIIE), now in its ninth edition, has also provided a platform for companies from other APEC economies to enter the Chinese market. This photo taken on Nov. 10, 2026 shows the exhibition area of Intelligent Industry and Information Technology of the 9th China International Import Expo in east China's Shanghai. (Xinhua/Han Xiaoyu) Australian dairy producer Bulla, which has participated in the expo every year since 2019, reached a direct-sourcing agreement with Chinese grocery platform Dingdong Fresh at the 2025 CIIE. Sam Zhang, who oversees international business at Bulla, said the company's exports to China exceeded 10 million Australian dollars (about 7 million dollars) in the financial year ended June 30, 2026. Beyond expanding market access, China has also worked with other APEC economies to promote development cooperation that benefits local communities. In Papua New Guinea, nearly three decades of cooperation with China on Juncao (the herbal plant for growing edible mushrooms) technology have created new income opportunities for rural households. First introduced to the country's Eastern Highlands Province in 1997, the technology has since been promoted through demonstration centers and farmer training programs. With guidance from Chinese agricultural experts, local farmer Zaka Abori began cultivating edible mushrooms in February 2020. China's International Development Cooperation Agency reported in 2022 that she earned an annual income of 15,000 kina (about 4,240 dollars) from mushroom cultivation, about seven times the annual income of most families in the area engaged in coffee and vegetable farming. By March 2025, Juncao and upland rice technologies had been promoted in 20 districts across 10 provinces of Papua New Guinea, with 3,277 people trained. In April 2026, Prime Minister James Marape called for a major expansion of the partnership, citing its contributions to rural livelihoods and agricultural development. Hans Hendrischke, professor of Chinese business and management at the University of Sydney Business School, said APEC's priorities of openness, innovation and cooperation address fundamental challenges facing the Asia-Pacific region, from resisting protectionism and embracing new technologies to developing common rules for cooperation. item.title: APEC comes to Shenzhen: where "China Opportunity 2.0" meets the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
Explainer: APEC comes to Shenzhen: where "China Opportunity 2.0" meets the world This photo taken on Nov. 13, 2026 shows a view of Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. China will hold the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen from Nov. 18 to 19. (Xinhua/Liang Xu) BEIJING, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- Next week, the gaze of the Asia-Pacific will turn to a young metropolis in southern China that, about four decades ago, was little more than a quiet fishing village. Shenzhen will play host to the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting -- the first time in 12 years that China has hosted the top event of the region's highest-level, most extensive and most influential economic cooperation mechanism. China officially joined APEC in 1991. Shenzhen, adjacent to Hong Kong, will become the third Chinese city after Shanghai and Beijing to welcome this gathering. Its rise over the past few decades stands as a miracle in the annals of global development, demonstrating what the Chinese people can achieve. When Shenzhen was designated a special economic zone in 1980, its GDP stood at just 270 million yuan (around 40.2 million U.S. dollars). By 2025, that figure had soared to 3.87 trillion yuan, trailing only Shanghai and Beijing. China's choice of Shenzhen mirrors a pattern common to other APEC economies, which tend to favor national capitals, major economic or technological hubs, or internationally renowned tourist destinations as host cities. For the 2026 APEC "China Year," China has set openness, innovation and cooperation as its three priorities. They echo the very forces that have shaped Shenzhen's development: openness is the city's defining feature, innovation its greatest strength, and cooperation a driving force behind its continued growth. An aerial drone photo taken on Oct. 20, 2026 shows a cargo ship sailing toward Yantian Port in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua) MARKET FOR THE WORLD Shenzhen's rise over more than forty years owes much to China's reform and opening up. One of the country's first special economic zones, Shenzhen has been a city of opportunity from the very beginning, pioneering one move after another. Countless entrepreneurs and innovators have gone there to pursue their ambitions, international investors have established a presence, and Chinese companies such as BYD and Huawei have grown from local businesses into global players. Shenzhen's tale has unfolded in step with the country's opening up. Today, China is expanding high-standard opening up. It has granted zero-tariff treatment to 63 countries, while remaining the world's second-largest importer for 17 consecutive years. In recent years, alongside further opening up the flow of goods, services, capital and talent, China has steadily expanded institutional opening up -- a key hallmark of high-standard opening up -- with respect to rules, regulations, management, and standards. The aim is to build a business environment that is transparent, stable and predictable, and to bring China's institutional framework into closer alignment with international standards. Shenzhen is a core city in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. Under "one country, two systems," the area's distinctive environment of three customs territories and three currencies has created valuable opportunities to explore the alignment of legal rules, cross-border professional practice, mutual recognition of qualifications, streamlined customs clearance and common standards. In this sense, the area serves as a testing ground for bridging different systems and improving institutional connectivity across the Asia-Pacific. This photo taken on Nov. 11, 2026 shows a coffee service area at the media center for the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Mao Siqian) INNOVATION DIVIDENDS Today's Shenzhen is internationally known for its technological prowess and is often dubbed "China's Silicon Valley." It now boasts more than 2 million professionals in science and technology. Yet when the special economic zone was first established in 1980, the city's entire pool of technical personnel consisted of just two people: a tractor mechanic and a veterinarian. This contrast captures the scale of Shenzhen's transformation. In recent years, Shenzhen's output of new energy vehicles, industrial robots and civilian drones has maintained double-digit growth for extended periods. The city has also become a popular destination for shoppers and technology enthusiasts looking to scour Huaqiangbei, its famed electronics market, for the latest products and cutting-edge innovations. China's industrial strengths in emerging sectors such as renewable energy and electric vehicles are no accident. They are the result of years of technological accumulation, well-developed industrial supply chains, and the opportunities created by a vast domestic market. If the "China Opportunity 1.0" of the past was largely about offering the world market dividends via China's enormous consumer market and low-cost production factors, today's "China Opportunity 2.0" is about delivering even greater market dividends while generating innovation dividends through technological progress and industrial upgrading. In China, businesses from around the world can quickly find partners to work with across the entire process, from research and development and prototype testing to mass production. Companies can tap into the Chinese market while strengthening their competitiveness in global markets. Seeing these advantages, foreign companies have increasingly moved beyond simply selling their products in China in recent years. Many have also established research and development centers and regional headquarters in the country. In 2025, 14,000 new foreign-invested enterprises were established in China's scientific research and technical services sector, a year-on-year increase of 27.2 percent. This photo taken on Nov. 3, 2026 shows a view of Shennan Avenue in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Liang Xu) COOPERATION FOR SHARED PROSPERITY The ocean connects rather than divides. Linked by the Pacific, the Asia-Pacific is one of the world's most dynamic economic regions, with deeply integrated regional economies and closely interconnected industrial and supply chains. Cooperation underpins the shared prosperity of the Asia-Pacific and is essential to building an Asia-Pacific community. Against a backdrop of rising unilateralism and protectionism, one of China's most important responsibilities as APEC host is to help bring economies back to the path of openness and cooperation. With global challenges -- climate change, food and energy security, demographic shifts and development imbalances -- intertwined and compounding, no single economy can prosper alone. Over the past year, the 2026 APEC "China Year" has produced substantial results. Working with other APEC member economies, China has organized more than 300 APEC meetings and events, which covered a wide range of areas, including trade, tourism, small and medium-sized enterprises, and energy. They helped build consensus on a series of areas for cooperation. Next week in Shenzhen, participating economies are expected to build on that consensus and deliver more practical outcomes in key areas such as trade, connectivity, the digital economy and artificial intelligence. Such progress would provide fresh impetus for economic growth and prosperity across the Asia-Pacific and beyond. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Shenzhen opens its doors wider to the Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
Shenzhen opens its doors wider to the Asia-Pacific Shenzhen, a coastal city in south China's Guangdong Province, will host the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting from Nov. 18 to 19. Shenzhen has grown from a fishing village into an international metropolis and much of that came from openness and cooperation across the Asia-Pacific region. Now the city is giving back, contributing to the region's development with renewed confidence. Chinese President Xi Jinping extended an invitation to the world at the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Gyeongju, South Korea, last November. "We look forward to all parties gathering in Shenzhen next year to jointly discuss development plans for the Asia-Pacific region and create a bright future for it," Xi said. As a window into China's reform and opening up, Shenzhen offers the world a glimpse of a more open and inclusive China. Visitors pose for photos with an APEC-themed display at Lianhuashan Park in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (People's Daily Online/Wang Xing) Visitors from around the world are flocking to Huaqiangbei, known as "China's No. 1 Electronics Street," to shop for products such as AI glasses, drones and 3D printers. Goods from the street now reach more than 190 countries and regions. The hub receives an average of more than 7,000 foreign visitors a day, and its annual sales exceed 400 billion yuan (about $60 billion). A similar scene is playing out in the robot block of Shenzhen's Longgang district. "In Shenzhen, I saw a picture of the future," said Emaunel Cardoso, a South American buyer shopping for a robot dog. He hopes to work with Chinese firms on materials and machinery. Visa-free policies, including 240-hour visa-free transit, have boosted international travel to the city. The number of foreign nationals entering and leaving China through Shenzhen ranked second nationwide in 2025. Meanwhile, Shenzhen's ports handled 273 million passenger trips, the highest figure in the country. APEC-themed flags hang on the robot block in Longgang district, Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (People's Daily Online/Wang Xing) Cargo is moving faster too. At Shenzhen airport's international cargo center, customs offers advance declaration and round-the-clock clearance by appointment for time-sensitive imports. So far this year, Shenzhen Airport Customs has cleared 8,500 tonnes of fresh produce and live seafood from APEC economies, including durians from Malaysia and wax apples from Thailand. The surge in travelers and cargo underscores the growing confidence of global investors in Shenzhen's business environment. As the global landscape shifts, Asia-Pacific economies are further opening their markets and building stronger consensus on win-win development. At the world's first robot 6S store in Shenzhen, a Malaysian businesswoman's smart coffee machines are popular among consumers. Drawn by China's incentives for foreign investment, she set up business in Shenzhen. Strong sales of her smart office products highlight the appeal of the Chinese market, and several Asia-Pacific firms have established operations in the city since the start of this year. Chinese companies are expanding overseas as well. The Longgang Enterprise Internationalization Service Base has served 9,494 companies looking to grow abroad, releasing orders worth more than 13.5 billion yuan (about $1.9 billion) and facilitating intent agreements worth a further 1 billion yuan, according to Li Qun, deputy general manager of Shenzhen Longgang Industrial Investment Service Group Co., Ltd. Photo shows APEC-themed displays on Shennan Avenue in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. (People's Daily Online/Wang Xing) China's trade with other APEC economies rose 23.9 percent year on year to 24.07 trillion yuan in the first three quarters of 2026. As of 2025, China had become the largest trading partner of 13 APEC economies. During the 2026 APEC "China Year," some 300 events are expected to take place across multiple cities in China, underscoring the country's commitment to multilateralism and regional economic integration. Across the Asia-Pacific, the benefits of greater openness are spreading further and faster. The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is now in force for all 15 members, with tariffs on more than 90 percent of goods traded within the region due to be eliminated over the coming decades. The China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol was signed in October 2025. Openness is a sure path for Asia-Pacific countries to achieve common prosperity. Amid global turbulence, only by expanding opening up and deepening cooperation can regional economies provide greater certainty and create new opportunities for the Asia-Pacific and the world. "Only by working together can Asia-Pacific countries, like passengers on the same boat, sail toward a better future," said Rinaldo Hartanto, a young Indonesian artist working in Shenzhen. item.title: How Chinese innovation drives shared growth from Shenzhen to Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
How Chinese innovation drives shared growth from Shenzhen to Asia-Pacific * Shenzhen offers a snapshot of this vibrant high-tech trade story. Total R&D spending in the city grew at an average annual rate of 12.9 percent from 2020 to 2024, and R&D intensity reached 6.67 percent, the highest among Chinese cities. The Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou innovation cluster has also topped the Global Innovation Index rankings. * Cooperation between Shenzhen and its Asia-Pacific partners advances along a well-defined track, featuring manufacturing, research and talent development, and the practical application of technology, said Chen Jiaxi, vice president of the Shenzhen Reform and Opening Up Executive Leadership Academy. * "The Shenzhen meeting will send a clear signal: China's commitment to high-standard opening up, to sharing opportunities with the Asia-Pacific, and to multilateralism remains firm," said Chen, who is also a professor at Shenzhen University. SHENZHEN, Nov. 14 (Xinhua) -- From a battery anode materials plant built from scratch in Indonesia to a surgical robot in a Kuala Lumpur operating room and solar panels atop a century-old Thai university, companies from China's southern tech hub of Shenzhen have established a presence across the Asia-Pacific region. Next week, as Shenzhen in Guangdong Province hosts the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," the innovative, collaborative approach that Shenzhen embodies will take center stage. The numbers are significant. China's goods trade with other APEC members reached 26.29 trillion yuan (about 3.9 trillion U.S. dollars) in 2025, or nearly 60 percent of its total foreign trade, according to the General Administration of Customs. High-tech goods are an increasingly strong link: China's exports of such products to other APEC members rose 8.1 percent to 4.63 trillion yuan in 2025. Shenzhen offers a snapshot of this vibrant high-tech trade story. Total R&D spending in the city grew at an average annual rate of 12.9 percent from 2020 to 2024, and R&D intensity reached 6.67 percent, the highest among Chinese cities. The Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou innovation cluster has also topped the Global Innovation Index rankings. Cooperation between Shenzhen and its Asia-Pacific partners advances along a well-defined track, featuring manufacturing, research and talent development, and the practical application of technology, said Chen Jiaxi, vice president of the Shenzhen Reform and Opening Up Executive Leadership Academy. "The Shenzhen meeting will send a clear signal: China's commitment to high-standard opening up, to sharing opportunities with the Asia-Pacific, and to multilateralism remains firm," said Chen, who is also a professor at Shenzhen University. A drone photo shows an exterior view of PT Indonesia BTR New Energy Material (PT BTR) at Kendal Industrial Park in Central Java province, Indonesia, Aug. 7, 2024. (Xinhua/Xu Qin) BUILDING LOCALLY BTR New Material Group (BTR), a Shenzhen-based battery materials maker, opened an anode material plant in Indonesia's Kendal Industrial Park in August 2024 -- the first overseas anode production base built by a Chinese company in the sector, said He Xueqin, the group's chairman. Before this plant, Indonesia had no lithium-ion battery anode manufacturing industry at all, He said. Then-Indonesian president Joko Widodo attended the opening, saying it brought the country a step closer to building an electric-vehicle ecosystem, the Economic Daily reported at the time. Two years on, a second phase is in full operation, doubling annual capacity to 160,000 tonnes. The Indonesian subsidiary's revenue jumped 161 percent year on year to 1.71 billion yuan in the first half of 2026, supplying battery makers in Japan, the Republic of Korea, Europe and the United States. Before the plant, Indonesia had already built a cathode materials industry from its nickel resources, and BTR added the anode link. "By 2026, separator and electrolyte production has also landed in Indonesia, completing the four main battery materials and laying a solid foundation for the electric-vehicle ecosystem," He said. The deeper shift is what BTR calls "chain-style overseas expansion," with the company having urged its strategic suppliers to move with it, helping them with local research, assessment and site selection. Packaging and crucible suppliers have already set up operations in Indonesia. Shenzhen SED Industry Co., Ltd. (SED), a subsidiary of China Electronics Corporation, is exporting plant-building capability itself. For an optical module project in Thailand, its design team analyzed years of local climate data rather than copying domestic designs, adding safeguards against heat and humidity in everything from equipment selection to insulation and cleanroom airtightness. At an electronics plant in Thailand's 304 Industrial Park, SED applied digital technology across design, construction and operations. Construction clashes fell by more than 95 percent, accidents by over 80 percent, and the plant went from blueprint to completion in just 270 days. The company now has more than 500 staff and over 1,300 overseas supply chain partners across APEC economies including Thailand, Vietnam and Malaysia, SED said. Staff members patrol at a plant of Shenzhen SED Industry Co., Ltd. (SED), a subsidiary of China Electronics Corporation, in Thailand in March 2025. (China Electronics Corporation/Handout via Xinhua) RESEARCH AND TALENT New plants need people who can run, maintain and improve them. Shenzhen's ties with the region are therefore extending beyond production lines into laboratories and classrooms. As of March 2026, BGI Group, a Shenzhen-based life science and genomics organization, had jointly trained students with more than 80 universities at home and abroad, including Chulalongkorn University and Mahidol University in Thailand, the University of Indonesia and the University of Malaya. These programs involved 4,490 students in total, 2,503 of them at master's or doctoral level. Such training is tied to research. With Chulalongkorn University, BGI is working on population aging, gut microbiome studies and thalassemia. In Indonesia, BGI signed an agreement in September 2026 with the health ministry's center for biomedical and health genomics to support the Biomedical and Genome Science Initiative, the country's first national genome program, covering joint research, platform development and local training. BGI describes its approach as "using projects to build disciplines, industries and talent." Since 2018, BGI has run 13 national-level training programs for more than 360 mid- and senior-level biotech professionals from Belt and Road partner countries, almost 60 percent of them from APEC members, and several alumni have become senior public health officials at home, the company said. Surgeons perform a robot-assisted surgery in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, in September 2026. (Yuanhua Tech/Handout via Xinhua) TECHNOLOGY ON THE GROUND The ultimate test of sci-tech cooperation is whether it can serve local needs and improve everyday life. In a Kuala Lumpur operating room, orthopaedic surgeon Rajiv Rampal guided a Shenzhen-developed robot through a hip replacement. The machine, developed by Shenzhen-based Yuanhua Robotics, Perception and AI Technologies Ltd. (Yuanhua Tech) and manufactured in Hong Kong, completed its first Malaysian operation in July and had performed 21 procedures by early September. Unlike many surgical robots that are tied to specific implant brands, the Shenzhen robot runs on an open platform: all 21 operations used international-brand implants familiar to local doctors. AI algorithms plan for different implant brands, achieving sub-millimeter placement without changing surgeons' routines. "Let the machine adapt to the doctor, not the doctor to the machine," a Yuanhua Tech official said. Shenzhen's rapid technological innovation, coupled with Hong Kong's international quality control standards, gives Malaysia access to cutting-edge medical technology, an official with the Malaysian Chinese-language daily Kwong Wah Yit Poh said. At century-old Mahidol University in Thailand, 41 campus buildings are topped with solar panels. Huawei describes the project as the Asia-Pacific's largest single-site commercial and industrial solar-plus-storage system. This project serves a national goal. Thailand announced at the COP26 climate summit in 2021 that it would achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, and has encouraged rooftop solar via incentives and tighter safety standards. The university chose Huawei's smart photovoltaic solution: 15 megawatts of solar capacity, 600 kilowatt-hours of storage and optimisers, which is expected to save around 2.3 million U.S. dollars a year and cut carbon emissions by 11,000 tonnes. The optimisers allow more panels across the 41 rooftops and lift power output by 10 percent, while the storage provides backup power. The campus is part of a wider footprint. By early 2025, Huawei's digital power business had served over 1,000 Thai enterprises and installed 6 gigawatts of solar inverters, helping generate more than 6 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity and cut carbon dioxide emissions by more than 5 million tonnes, said Yu Junxiang, an official with Huawei's arm in Thailand. Taken together, Chen said, these cases show how Shenzhen, an urban test case for Chinese modernization, can serve a region: openness breeds cooperation and innovation drives shared growth, offering Asia-Pacific economies a viable path to build consensus, narrow development gaps and achieve shared prosperity. item.title: China willing to further boost political mutual trust with Thailand, says Chinese premier
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14
China willing to further boost political mutual trust with Thailand, says Chinese premier Chinese Premier Li Qiang holds talks with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, Thailand, Nov. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen) BANGKOK, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Friday that China is willing to work with Thailand to further consolidate the foundation of political mutual trust, support each other's core interests and major concerns, tap cooperation potential in various fields and deliver more tangible results to better benefit the peoples of both countries. Li made the remarks when meeting with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul. He said Chinese President Xi Jinping met with Anutin during the Thai PM's official visit to China in July, and the two leaders jointly charted the course for the development of China-Thailand relations. Li said that, with his visit to Thailand, the prime ministers of the two countries have exchanged visits within four months, fully demonstrating the high level of bilateral relations. Noting that both China and Thailand are at an important stage of national development, Li said China firmly supports the Thai government in smoothly carrying out its work. China is willing to work with Thailand to make good use of mechanisms such as the "2+2" strategic dialogue between foreign and defense ministers and the joint committee on economic and trade cooperation, Li said. China stands ready to work with Thailand to strengthen the alignment of development strategies, advance high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and key projects such as the China-Thailand railway, and accelerate consultations on a new five-year plan for economic and trade cooperation, Li said. He added that China is ready to promote the early realization of mutual protection of geographical indication products, and expand cooperation in such fields as finance, new energy, semiconductors, and artificial intelligence, so as to achieve mutual benefit and win-win outcomes at a higher level. China is ready to import more quality products from Thailand and encourages Chinese companies to invest and do business in the Southeast Asian country, he said, adding that China hopes the Thai side will provide a fair, stable and predictable business environment for Chinese companies. The two sides, Li said, should also strengthen exchanges and cooperation in areas including disaster prevention and mitigation, water resources management, education, tourism and media, and step up efforts to combat illegal and criminal activities, to enhance the people's sense of gain from China-Thailand cooperation. At present, the international situation remains fraught with instability and uncertainty, Li said, noting that China is willing to strengthen coordination and cooperation with Thailand under multilateral frameworks including China-ASEAN, the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation, the United Nations, the World Trade Organization and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, so as to contribute to global peace and development. For his part, Anutin said Thailand attaches great importance to its relations with China and is committed to advancing all-round cooperation between the two countries and continuously elevating the Thailand-China comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership to new heights, bringing greater benefits to the two peoples. Thailand is willing to strengthen high-level exchanges with China, make good use of mechanisms such as the "2+2" strategic dialogue between foreign and defense ministers of the two countries, expand bilateral trade, and deepen mutually beneficial cooperation in fields including agriculture, finance, connectivity, electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, e-commerce, and science and technology, said the Thai prime minister. Thailand is ready to continue providing a favorable business environment for Chinese enterprises investing in Thailand, strengthen law enforcement and security cooperation with China to combat online gambling, telecom and online fraud among other crimes, ensure the safety of Chinese tourists, and deepen people-to-people and cultural exchanges to consolidate the foundation of public friendship, Anutin said. Thailand supports China's successful hosting of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting and stands ready to work with China to ensure the success of the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation Leaders' Meeting, making new contributions to regional stability, development and prosperity, said the Thai prime minister. Following the talks, the two leaders witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents covering the fields including the automotive industry, vocational education, agriculture, customs and security. Chinese Premier Li Qiang holds talks with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, Thailand, Nov. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Yin Bogu) Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.
